title: Pay‐for‐prominence: The (un)intended consequences of monetary incentives on employees' networks and attrition
authors: Alessandro Iorio; Giuseppe Soda; Brandy Aven
affiliations: Department of Management and Technology Bocconi University Milan Italy; ICRIOS Bocconi University Milan Italy; Tepper School of Business Carnegie Mellon University Pittsburgh Pennsylvania USA
abstract: Abstract Research Summary We introduce the concept of pay‐for‐prominence , a system where employees are monetarily incentivized to become knowledge hubs in the intrafirm network and examine its effects on employees' networks and attrition. Integrating social network theory with relational incentives theory, we argue that pay‐for‐prominence motivates strategic networking behaviors that lead to the emergence of prominent connectors. However, these changes are associated with higher attrition as employees are preoccupied with networking, thus suggesting a trade‐off between enhanced connectivity in the short term and the risk of network fragmentation in the long term. Using a field quasi‐experiment in a multinational firm, we show that organizations can successfully incentivize employees' network prominence, but doing so may produce unintended consequences. Managerial Summary We examine the impact of using monetary incentives to encourage employees to become knowledge hubs in the workplace informal network—a term we label pay‐for‐prominence. We find that offering monetary rewards based on network metrics encourages employees to broaden their connections, enhancing knowledge flows within the firm. However, employees who become more socially prominent experience higher attrition than those who do not, as they become preoccupied with networking. Therefore, while incentivizing networking can improve knowledge sharing, it also requires careful management to avoid unintended consequences, such as the exit of key players that could cause fragmentation of the social network. Managers should weigh the benefits of increased connectivity against the risks of fragmentation when designing incentive programs aimed at fostering informal networks.

title: Public Administration and the Crisis of American Democracy
authors: Donald F. Kettl
affiliations: University of Maryland School of Public Policy College Park Maryland USA
abstract: ABSTRACT The field of public administration stands amid genuine crisis. Americans don't trust government or its administrators. Elected officials have attacked the career service as agents of the “deep state” and, though it might be hard to admit, many of public administration's critics have a point. Government's performance too often falls short of what people expect, practitioners too often seem too unresponsive to elected officials, and researchers too often seem to have only fuzzy guidance for practitioners. However, public administration undoubtedly is more important now than ever in translating public goals into effective action, and in bringing to life the democratic aspirations Madison and his colleagues wished for the country at its founding. The field urgently needs new strategies and tactics for solving the new generation of puzzles the country faces. In coming together, practitioners and researchers build on these puzzles to chart an exciting road forward.

title: Why Zoning Is Too Restrictive
authors: Jack Favilukis; Jaehee Song
affiliations: Sauder School of Business, The University of British Columbia, Vancouver, British Columbia V6T 1Z2, Canada; Leeds School of Business, University of Colorado, Boulder, Colorado 80309
abstract: Economists estimate that zoning regulations raise house prices, lower productivity, and reduce aggregate welfare, yet regulations remain widespread. We develop and solve a model in which fragmented zoning authority leads to overly strict regulations: Homeowners impose stricter regulations to mitigate local congestion but fail to internalize the broader impact on metro-wide affordability. Empirically, the Herfindahl-Hirschman index of local governments explains 12% of the variation in zoning restrictiveness. Using an instrument based on 19th-century municipal fragmentation, we show that greater fragmentation leads to stricter zoning and higher housing costs. These findings suggest that centralizing zoning decisions could alleviate housing affordability challenges. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. title: From Winning to Giving: The Effect of Gold Medals in Crowdsourcing Contests
authors: Shan Liu; Fan Zhang; Jing Wang; Baojun Gao
affiliations: School of Management, Xi’an Jiaotong University, Xi’an 710049, China; Department of Information Systems, Business Statistics, and Operations Management, School of Business and Management, The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Hong Kong, China; Business School of Science and Technology, Wuhan University, Wuhan 430072, China
abstract: We examine how users respond to winning symbolic awards in online crowdsourcing contests. Our setting is a machine learning competition platform that grants symbolic medals to recognize participants’ contest achievements. Employing a regression discontinuity design, we find that gold medal winners participate less in subsequent contests but engage more in prosocial activities, evidenced by a greater volume and length of posts, as well as more substantial and frequent code contributions. In contrast, bronze and silver medals do not seem to exert a significant influence on recipients’ subsequent behaviors. Drawing on self-determination theory and the needs-as-motives hypothesis, we provide evidence that need-driven goal shifting plays an important role in driving the dual effects of gold medals—diminished contest participation but enhanced prosocial contributions. Further analyses reveal that winners with previous competition medals are more likely to favor contributing content over competing again, whereas winners with more prior contribution medals are less inclined to further increase contributions. Moreover, team winners exhibit a lower tendency than solo winners to shift their efforts from competition to contribution. We add to the symbolic awards literature by uncovering a novel goal-shifting effect induced by contest medals, where award receipt redirects user effort from the focal rewarded domain to other forms of platform engagement. title: From Bytes to Bites: Examining the Online and Offline Spillover Impacts of Online Food Delivery Platform Subscriptions
authors: Jaeho Myeong; Yongjin Park; Francis Joseph Costello; Keongtae Kim; Jae-Hyeon Ahn
affiliations: College of Business and Economics, Hanyang University ERICA, Ansan 15588, Republic of Korea; College of Business, City University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Nova School of Business and Economics, Universidade NOVA de Lisboa, Campus de Carcavelos, 2775-405 Carcavelos, Portugal; Chinese University of Hong Kong Business School, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; College of Business, Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST), Seoul 02455, Republic of Korea; and Seoul Business School, Seoul School of Integrated Sciences & Technologies (aSSIST) University, Seoul 03767, Republic of Korea
abstract: With the rapid expansion of online food delivery (OFD) platforms, subscription models have emerged as a strategic tool to retain users and shape consumption behavior. Despite their growing prevalence, the broader impacts of these subscriptions—both within the OFD sector and across downstream consumer activities—remain underexplored. Leveraging a difference-in-differences approach and a large-scale individual-level transaction data set, we identify a significant shift in consumption from a competing platform to the focal platform following the introduction of a subscription service. This shift did not result in cannibalization; instead, overall food consumption within the OFD market increased. Geospatial analysis shows that subscribers were more likely to engage in offline spillovers, including increased local dining and activity in nearby noncompeting economic sectors. These patterns suggest that subscriptions in physical services, like OFD, not only reshape digital engagement, but also, they influence consumer mobility and stimulate localized economic ecosystems. Mechanistic testing supports the interpretation that these effects are driven by increased variety-seeking behavior for offline restaurants that predominantly serve non-OFD cuisines within a proximal location, suggesting that such behavior is constrained by transportation costs. Overall, this study offers novel insights into how subscription models in physical service platforms can expand market demand, foster crosschannel engagement, and generate positive spillovers in adjacent sectors. The findings offer actionable guidance for platform designers and policymakers to enhance consumer welfare and support local economic vitality. They also provide new evidence for restaurants that additional platform usage costs may be offset by latent economic benefits from heightened consumer engagement. This paper was accepted by D. J. title: Information Transparency, Choice Confidence, and Customer Retention: Field and Laboratory Evidence from Markets for Credence Goods
authors: Zhi (Aaron) Cheng; Ting Li; Paul A. Pavlou
affiliations: Department of Management, London School of Economics, London WC2A 2AE, United Kingdom; Rotterdam School of Management, Erasmus University, Rotterdam 3062 PA, Netherlands; University of Miami Business School, Miami, Florida 33146
abstract: How does information transparency affect customer retention in markets where quality is difficult to verify? Conventional wisdom suggests that transparency intensifies price competition and increases customer churn. We challenge this view by showing that acquisition-stage transparency can strengthen retention in markets for credence goods characterized by delayed feedback and persistent uncertainty, where customers revisit their decisions without clear quality signals. We develop a transparency-confidence-retention framework, in which transparency at acquisition builds choice confidence, a psychological switching cost that anchors customers to their initial decisions. Using 83,835 auto insurance contracts from a European insurer and multiple identification strategies, we find that customers acquired through transparent channels are 4.6%–11.8% less likely to churn than those acquired through less transparent channels. A randomized, controlled experiment with 1,515 participants shows that transparency reduces customer churn primarily by strengthening choice confidence rather than increasing conventional switching costs, such as brand trust or product fit. Decomposing transparency into attribute, comparative, and evaluative dimensions reveals that evaluative transparency exerts the strongest influence. Analyses of boundary conditions indicate that the retention effect of transparency is amplified when public and private signals remain congruent with earlier informational cues. These findings reconceptualize transparency as a relational mechanism that fosters decisional assurance and stabilizes retention under quality uncertainty. authors: Jin Liu; Xingchen Xu; Xi Nan; Yongjun Li; Yong Tan
affiliations: University of Science and Technology of China School of Management, Department of Management Science, Hefei, Anhui, China; University of Washington, Information Systems and Operations Management, Seattle, Washington, 98195-0005, United States; University of Washington, Michael G. abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based generative AI systems are general-purpose tools capable of augmenting or even automating a wide range of job functions, positioning them to reshape labor market dynamics. However, predicting their precise impact a priori is challenging, given AI’s simultaneous effects on both demand and supply, as well as the strategic responses of market participants. Leveraging an extensive dataset from a leading online labor platform, we document a pronounced displacement effect and an overall contraction in submarkets where required skills closely align with core LLM functionalities. Although demand and supply both decline, the reduction in supply is comparatively smaller, thereby intensifying competition among freelancers. Notably, further analysis shows that this heightened competition is especially pronounced in programming-intensive submarkets. This pattern is attributed to skill-transition effects: by lowering the human-capital barrier to programming, ChatGPT enables incumbent freelancers to enter programming tasks. Moreover, these transitions are not homogeneous, with high-skilled freelancers contributing disproportionately to the shift. Our findings illuminate the multifaceted impacts of general-purpose AI on labor markets, highlighting not only the displacement of certain occupations but also the inducement of skill transitions within the labor supply. These insights offer practical implications for policymakers, platform operators, and workers.

title: Campaigns That Click: Unleashing the Power of Push Notifications on Mobile Apps
authors: Zhuping Liu; Bicheng Yang; Subodha Kumar
affiliations: Baruch College Zicklin School of Business, Marketing and International Business, New York, New York, United States; The Hong Kong Polytechnic University Faculty of Business, management and marketing, Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Temple University, Supply Chain, Information Systems, Marketing, and Statistics, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, United States
abstract: As mobile apps increasingly mediate digital engagement, push notifications have emerged as a key tool for directing user attention, yet systematic evidence on their behavioral and ecosystem-level effects remains limited. Using data from over 200 push campaigns and 60 million user-campaign observations on a leading U.S. mobile-offer marketplace, we combine large-scale observational analyses with controlled experiments to study how push notifications shape user engagement. We find that push notifications significantly increase same-day click-throughs to advertised merchants, with substantial heterogeneity across merchant characteristics, user characteristics, message design, and delivery timing. Beyond focal-merchant responses, notifications are associated with increased engagement with non-advertised merchants both within and across categories, suggesting that push notifications reshape attention across the marketplace ecosystem. Both the large-scale empirical analysis and controlled experiments yield evidence consistent with two complementary mechanisms—content-driven processing of notification information and reminder-based attention activation. The results also identify attentional saturation as a key boundary condition—repeated exposure produces diminishing responsiveness and may even reduce engagement at high notification frequencies. These findings position push notifications as a mobile-native attention-allocation lever that platforms can strategically deploy, while underscoring the need to balance engagement gains against user fatigue and attention costs.

title: Mobile Location-based Recommendation Systems and Local Businesses: Evidence from the Restaurant Industry
authors: Jin Soo Han; Gunwoong Lee; Keongtae Kim
affiliations: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology College of Business, IT Management, Seoul, Korea (the Republic of); Korea University, Management Information Systems, Seongbuk-gu, Seoul, Korea (the Republic of); Chinese University of Hong Kong, Decisions, Operations and Technology, Shatin, Hong Kong
abstract: We investigate the impact of mobile location-based recommendation systems (MLBRS) on the performance of local businesses. Leveraging a comprehensive dataset of 16,720 restaurants and quasi-experimental variation generated by the official launch of a leading MLBRS, we employ a 2-Stage Least Squares instrumental-variable framework to estimate the effect of algorithmic exposure on consumer engagement. Our analysis reveals that a 1% increase in exposure is associated with a 0.078% increase in clicks; separately, a 1% increase in clicks is associated with a 0.053% increase in visit intentions. Importantly, the estimated exposure effect is larger for geographically disadvantaged restaurants, but primarily at the discovery stage (clicks). This pattern highlights a boundary condition of MLBRS: algorithmic visibility can aid, but it does not by itself resolve the uncertainty involved in acting on a recommendation. Downstream conversion is stronger when restaurants provide richer digital information and reputation signals, including consumer reviews and owner-curated information such as photos and menus. Auxiliary credit-card sales data from a restricted Seoul subsample provide consistent evidence of a positive association between algorithmic exposure and revenue, suggesting that MLBRS can shape the connection of online recommendations to offline economic outcomes.

title: Risk Assessment of an Illegal Laboratory in Reedley, California, Using Geospatial Analysis of Open‐Source Epidemic Intelligence Data
authors: Atalay Goshu Muluneh; Rebecca Dawson; Jared Edgeworth; Natalie L. Cain; Ashley Quigly; Aye Moa; Samsung Lim; Chandini Raina MacIntyre
affiliations: Biosecurity Program, The Kirby Institute, Faculty of Medicine and Health the University of New South Wales Sydney Australia; Victorian Infectious Diseases Reference Laboratory Royal Melbourne Hospital, Doherty Institute for Infection and Immunity Melbourne Australia; School of Civil and Environmental Engineering University of New South Wales Sydney Australia; College of Public Service & Community Solutions and College of Health Solutions Arizona State University Tempe United States
abstract: ABSTRACT An illegal laboratory discovered in Reedley, California, in December 2022 was in a warehouse, operating without a license, handling about a thousand transgenic mice, chemicals, and possibly over 20 pathogens, including vials labeled Ebola, which were never tested but destroyed. This study aimed to estimate epidemic signals around the Reedley illegal laboratory using open‐source epidemic intelligence data. We utilized data from EPIWATCH, from October 2021 to October 2023, a year prior to and a year after the establishment of the illegal laboratory. The spatial pattern of outbreak signals was analyzed using hotspot analysis, and the distances of outbreak signals from the laboratory were measured. In California, an upward trend in outbreak signals of pathogens associated with the laboratory was noted in December 2022, April 2023, and August 2023. In the hotspot analysis, California and eight other states in the United States (US) were identified as hotspots. Narrative evidence revealed the presence of a sick employee working in the laboratory, whose child also became ill. Changes in disease patterns reported in California or the US in the year following the establishment of the illegal laboratory may or may not be linked to the illegal laboratory. A subsequent illegal lab linked to Reedley was identified in Las Vegas in 2026, highlighting the ongoing threat to biosecurity. EPIWATCH geospatial and temporal analysis can enhance the public health risk assessment of threats associated with illegal laboratories, especially when there is no available testing or reporting.

title: Organization and the Signature of Power
authors: Mitchell Dean; Stefan Schwarzkopf
abstract: This paper introduces the ‘signature of power’ as a framework to enhance the understanding of politics in organizational studies. We argue for an understanding of contemporary forms of power as a signature that connects and divides two constellations: juridical-political sovereignty (supreme authority) on one side, and economic-managerial government (practical regulation) on the other. These poles have analogies in organizational theory dichotomies like formal versus informal, and institution versus network. The signature of power serves as a heuristic – a discovery mechanism – that enables scholars to navigate and integrate these opposing forces without reducing them to one dominant paradigm. The framework is articulated through four analytical strategies: analytics of government (local, immanent power practices), genealogy of order (historical foundations of governing orders), archaeology of glory (rituals and symbols of supreme authority), and analytics of authority (formal organizational hierarchies and operations). These strategies and their distinct relationships provide a more coherent analytical framework for a multi-paradigm approach to understanding power relations, resistance, and organizational forms. The paper tests this analytic framework through a study of the corporation as a ‘signature of power’ that bridges economic-managerial and juridical-political forms and is shaped by historical shifts and legal innovations. Addressing potential critiques, the paper emphasizes the framework’s adaptability to resistance and its applicability to diverse organizational contexts. This conceptualization encourages intellectual plurality, fostering historically and conceptually informed insight into politics as a set of power-related organizational and institutional practices.

title: EXPRESS: Do You Lose When You Sell Loose? Impact of Unpackaged Sales on Profit and Waste
authors: Ismail Kirci; Dorothee Honhon; Alp Muharremoglu
abstract: Loose sales — the sale of unpackaged products by unit or weight — are frequently promoted as a way to reduce waste because they allow consumers to purchase exactly the quantity they want, rather than being constrained by the fixed quantities dictated by the pre-packaged format. We study a retailer selling a highly perishable product under two possible formats: fixed-size packages and/or loose. The retailer chooses prices and package size to maximize profit. Consumers perceive loose products as fresher, but they also incur an inconvenience cost arising from the additional time and effort required. For the retailer, loose sales carry a higher unit variable cost due to increased labor requirements. In a homogeneous market, we show that, if consumers place substantially higher value on the loose option and its cost is not significantly greater than that of packaged sale, the retailer can make more profit selling only loose at a high price to consumers who buy the quantity they desire. Otherwise, the retailer is better off selling packages of large size, forcing consumers to buy more than they desire to purchase. Interestingly, consumer waste can actually be greater when the product is sold exclusively in loose format. In a heterogeneous market with two consumer segments which differ in the magnitude of their consumption needs, three possible optimal strategies emerge: selling only loose to both segments, selling only (relatively small) packages to both segments, or selling (relatively large) packages to high-consumption needs consumers and selling loose to the low-consumption needs consumers. Our results also demonstrate that selling loose instead of or alongside packages can often be a win-win strategy, simultaneously boosting retailer profits and reducing consumer waste compared to selling only packages. However, in some cases, introducing loose sales may increase waste. These findings indicate that retailers may derive financial gains from offering products in loose form; however, they should ensure that the associated sustainability benefits are genuine before positioning it as a green strategy. Likewise, policymakers seeking to reduce food waste should carefully consider product- and market-specific conditions rather than promoting loose sales as a universally effective waste-reduction measure.

title: EXPRESS: Interoperability Meets Accountability: How Data Interoperability and Experiential Quality Influence Malpractice Lawsuits
authors: Sukrit Pal; David E. Cantor; Anand Nair
abstract: A persistent challenge that many patients continue to face is substandard care including errors in their medical records (Sharma et al., 2019). To address this situation, health information exchanges (HIE) have been established to seamlessly share patient data across organizations. In this study, we examine whether policy-driven support for data interoperability—operationalized through health information exchange (HIE) systems—is associated with increased malpractice liability. Drawing on the empowerment literature, we argue that greater operational transparency enabled by data sharing may empower patients to scrutinize care quality, thereby elevating the risk of litigation. Using an eight-year panel data set covering 952 U.S. hospitals from 2010 to 2017 and over 24,000 malpractice case filings, we find that HIE adoption is associated with a statistically significant 10.5% increase in malpractice lawsuits. However, this effect is moderated by hospitals’ experiential quality, as measured by patient-reported experiences of communication, empathy, and responsiveness. In hospitals with high experiential quality, the effect of HIE adoption on malpractice lawsuits is reduced by 20.4%, suggesting that positive patient interactions can reduce the legal risks associated with HIE adoption. Our findings highlight a critical trade-off. While data interoperability improves operational coordination and patient engagement, it can also elevate legal exposure. This research contributes to the operations management and public policy literature by reframing interoperability not just as a backend coordination tool but also as a patient-facing technological development with reputational and legal implications.

title: EXPRESS: From Chit-Chat to Conversion: Cost-Efficient Conversational Recommendation via Retrospective Learning and Isolated Reflection
authors: Jiahui Wang; Hongke Zhao; Likang Wu; Bing Lv; Ning Jia
abstract: Conversational recommendation systems help digital platforms elicit user preferences through multi-turn interaction, but they often face a practical tension between recommendation accuracy and interaction cost when users provide vague or low-information inputs. This study follows a design science approach to develop a cost-conscious conversational recommendation artifact for such ambiguous service encounters. The artifact is guided by two design principles. First, retrospective outcome-guided supervision uses successful historical conversion trajectories as downstream anchors for improving responses at earlier low-information states. Second, isolated reflection separates recommendation generation from consistency checking, enabling diagnostic regeneration when candidate responses conflict with previously stated user constraints. In implementation, the artifact instantiates these principles through parameter-efficient adaptation of open-source large language models and prompt-isolated role switching over a shared backbone model. We validate the artifact on three conversational recommendation datasets covering movie and e-commerce settings, using outcome efficacy, interaction efficiency, process analysis, ablation analysis, robustness checks, and human evaluation. Here, interaction efficiency refers to user-visible dialogue turns, while computational burden is reported separately through training, memory, and latency measurements. The empirical results show that the artifact improves recommendation effectiveness while maintaining a favorable balance between interaction burden and conversion outcomes under the tested conditions. Process-level analysis further characterizes how recommendation behavior evolves over the course of dialogue. This study contributes transferable design principles for embedding retrospective preference optimization and isolated reflection into conversational recommendation systems, offering operational guidance for platforms seeking to improve personalization under constraints on interaction cost.

title: EXPRESS: When Good Practices Go Too Far: Overshooting in Organizational Culture
authors: Francisco Brahm; Christoph Loch; Joaquin Poblete
abstract: Business research has examined how useful practices can be made to spread and develop in organizations. However, practices have been observed “overshooting”: either over-diffusing—too many employees adopt them, including some whose usage is unproductive; or becoming over-sophisticated—the practice becomes too elaborate, reducing organizational performance. Independent models of over-diffusion and over-sophistication have been proposed; this paper integrates both aspects in a simple, unified model of overshooting. We offer a cultural evolution model that studies how interaction dynamics among employees are able to diffuse and stabilize an equilibrium of underperforming cultural practices, at the same time over-developing the practice so its sophistication goes beyond productive levels. People adopt practices from others based on information about the practice’s productive value, but also influenced by social dynamics with other employees, such as status. Our model clarifies the circumstances in which over-diffusion and over-sophistication can arise, and how these two elements of overshooting relate to each other. We map our model in detail to two cases---process management practices (e.g., six sigma) and Uber's aggressive culture---and discuss the managerial implications.

title: EXPRESS: Participation Governance in Consumer and AI Co-creation: Whether to Intervene and How to Design It
authors: Mengxia Zhang; Brian Rongqing Han; Tianshu Sun; Lan Luo; Joseph M. Golden
abstract: Artificial intelligence reshapes digital mass customization by altering the structure of consumer co-creation. When consumers start from a draft generated by artificial intelligence rather than a blank canvas, outcomes are jointly determined by two stages: whether consumers initiate co-creation and, conditional on participation, how much refinement effort they exert. This separation makes participation a governable design margin—an issue that is largely muted in traditional blank-canvas customization, where participation and effort are tightly bundled. Partnering with a leading United States online retailer of personalized photo products, we study whether and how firm interventions at the participation stage shape downstream purchase outcomes. We develop a two-stage model in which, relative to a baseline with organic participation, a nudge lowers start-up frictions and expands voluntary entry, whereas a mandate serves as a strong boundary-case intervention that guarantees entry but can weaken how participation translates into purchase, generating a reach–efficiency trade-off. We examine these predictions in two randomized experiments. In Study 1, a light-touch nudge increases participation by 5.98 percentage points and raises revenue and order frequency. The evidence is consistent with gains arising primarily through expanded entry into consumer co-creation with artificial intelligence. In Study 2, mandates increase participation relative to nudges, but we find no clear evidence of additional gains in purchase or revisit intentions. Instead, mandates increase low-value participation, in which consumers exert minimal effort and report low purchase intention. Together, these findings show that in mass customization enabled by artificial intelligence, participation governance is a consequential design choice: firms must consider not only how many consumers initiate co-creation, but also whether the participation they induce creates downstream value.

title: EXPRESS: Harnessing Renewable Portfolio Standards for Sustainable Futures: An Empirical Examination of Spillover Effects
authors: Chunjie Zhao; Anqi Wu; Ramanathan Subramanyam
abstract: Given the importance of managing industrial energy consumption, setting standards and implementing policies that encourage renewable energy use is crucial for incentivizing sustainable firm practices. Public policy designs must align closely with firms’ environmental policies to help mitigate greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and support a sustainable future. While research on policy impacts on firm environmental performance and the supply chain's role in sustainability is growing, a critical, understudied effect is the spillover of government rules to supply chain partners and peer firms, especially those outside the direct purview of environmental regulations. This paper presents a novel approach that integrates data from the Carbon Disclosure Project (CDP) and the Renewable Portfolio Standards (RPS). The latter refers to state-driven initiatives that incentivize electricity consumption from eligible renewable resources. We examine the causal effects of state-level policies on firm-level GHG emission intensity, with particular emphasis on the spillover effects of policies on unregulated firms across markets. We break down emission intensity into Scope 1 and Scope 2 and capture facility-level data to analyze spillover effects in granular detail. Using a staggered difference-in-differences methodology, our analysis finds a promising negative association between RPS introduction and GHG emission intensity among unregulated firms across industries. Interestingly, firms headquartered in states with more conservative initial targets during RPS adoption and progressive, milestone-based implementation strategies have significantly lower GHG emission intensity than those headquartered in states with more aggressive initial targets or long-term absolute targets. Our findings have significant implications for developing environmental regulations and public policies aimed at reducing GHG emission intensity.

title: EXPRESS: What Drives Physician Efficiency? Evidence from Emergency Department Operations
authors: Raha Imanirad; Soroush Saghafian; Stephen J. Traub; Nicole R. Hodgson
abstract: Emergency department (ED) physicians play a critical role in healthcare, serving on the frontline of acute care delivery. Yet increasing demand, resource constraints, and growing patient complexity pose significant challenges to physician efficiency. In this study, we investigate the determinants of ED physician efficiency using a multi-stage framework. First, we apply Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) to measure individual physician efficiency based on data from 110,325 patient visits at a leading U.S. hospital. Second, we use a Tobit regression model to analyze how physician experience, shift familiarity, and patient severity influence physician efficiency. Third, we conduct comprehensive robustness checks, including omitted variable bias sensitivity analyses, permutation tests, and machine learning-based classification analyses, to address concerns regarding endogeneity and potential model misspecification. Our results show that physician efficiency increases with experience at a diminishing rate. Efficiency also varies with shift familiarity, with the estimated association weakening as physician experience increases. In addition, higher patient severity is associated with lower physician efficiency, consistent with the greater resource demands of caring for more clinically complex patients. This negative association is attenuated for more experienced physicians, suggesting that experienced physicians are better able to maintain efficiency when managing more demanding clinical conditions. Our findings offer actionable recommendations for improving ED operations. Staffing strategies that assign relatively more experienced physicians to higher-severity patients may help maintain physician efficiency, while shift familiarity may inform a scheduling strategy that emphasizes greater scheduling consistency for relatively less experienced physicians and greater flexibility for relatively more experienced physicians. Simulation results further illustrate the potential reductions in physician resource use associated with these strategies. Together, these findings highlight the value of evidence-based physician staffing and scheduling to improve physician efficiency in EDs.

title: Biased by sustainability? How cognitive biases shape procurement decisions under information equivocality
authors: Chiara Vagnini; Mariolina Longo; Matteo Mura
affiliations: University of Bologna Department of Management, , ,
abstract: Purpose Climate change introduces new informational asymmetries across supply chains, increasing managers' need to process sustainability-related information in procurement decisions. Such information is equivocal, making its interpretation challenging and increasing decision-makers’ susceptibility to cognitive biases. Building on organizational information-processing theory and behavioral decision-making research, this study examines how cognitive biases shape procurement decisions involving sustainability information. Design/methodology/approach We developed hypotheses on cognitive biases emerging from three characteristics of sustainability information: structural properties (risky choice framing, attribute framing, numeracy and anchoring), inferential dynamics (halo effect) and social influences (herd effect). We tested these hypotheses through between-subject vignette-based experiments depicting individual, one-shot procurement decisions. The experiments were conducted in person with 475 participants, including managers and students. Findings We found that sustainability-oriented procurement decisions are vulnerable to cognitive biases. In particular, biases induced by the structural properties of information produced the strongest effects across both managers and students, followed by distortions emerging from inferential dynamics. In contrast, socially driven distortions emerged only among students, suggesting that professional experience mitigates reliance on peer behavior. Originality/value This study extends organizational information-processing theory-based sustainable supply chain management research by demonstrating that individual-level cognitive biases shape the interpretation of sustainability information. In doing so, we characterize the interpretation stage as being sensitive to information architecture, inferential reasoning and, under conditions of social influence, the professional experience of the decision-maker. Finally, we provide guidance for designing sustainability information and procurement decision processes that reduce susceptibility to cognitive biases.

title: Reshaping Work: Job Reallocation and Job Attributes During the Great Resignation in Italy
authors: Francesco Suppressa; Chiara Franco; Tiziano Razzolini
affiliations: University of Pisa Pisa Italy; University of Siena, GLO, IZA, LABOR, and ASESD Siena Italy
abstract: ABSTRACT The Covid‐19 pandemic reshaped labor markets worldwide, including the emergence of the “Great Resignation” (GR). This study examines whether Italy's GR reflects labor force exits or job switching and identifies and explores which job attributes are associated with these reallocation patterns. Using Italian Labor Force Survey data, we construct a job‐switching indicator that aligns with administrative resignation trends and enables the exploration of potential determinants through a task‐based approach. Results are consistent with the interpretation that Italy's Great Resignation mainly reflects job reallocation across occupations characterized by differences in flexibility, meaning, and working conditions.

title: Follow the Money: The State and the Architecture of Union Funding
authors: Assaf S. Bondy
affiliations: Bristol Business School University of Bristol and Haifa University, Haifa. Bristol UK
abstract: ABSTRACT Trade unions need money to sustain the staff, infrastructure and activities on which all forms of union power depend, yet the financial dimensions of unions and their power have been largely overlooked in the comparative study of industrial relations. This article addresses the gap by using unions’ financial means as a revealing lens for understanding the role of the state in shaping union power. The comparison distinguished two ideal‐typical logics of state action behind union funding. Under indirect action, the state enables unions to convert membership into income, producing a tight coupling between union funds and organisational power. Under direct action, the state channels funds to unions on the basis of their recognised societal roles, decoupling income from membership. Systematised during the early decades of the twentieth century, these two action paths present fundamental transformations through liberalisation, leading to the financialisation and politicisation of union funding. By analysing the structures and changes in unions’ financial sustainability, this framework reveals the state's constitutive role in shaping and transforming union power.

title: It's in the Small Steps: Navigating Knotted Change‐Stability Tensions in Complex Collaborations
authors: Lea Stadtler; Luk N. Van Wassenhove
affiliations: Grenoble Ecole de Management; INSEAD
abstract: Abstract Addressing societal challenges requires collaborative arrangements that can adapt to changing environments while maintaining coherence. Existing research highlights collaborative responses to change, yet the processes through which such responses emerge remain poorly understood. Notably, collaborative change involves not only balancing change and stability but also navigating knotted collective‐individual tensions that arise in realigning interests, coordination structures, and operations. To advance understanding of these dynamics, we conduct an in‐depth longitudinal study of collaborative change in a cross‐sector disaster relief partnership. Across successive change stages, we identify stability drivers emerging from collective‐individual tensions that prompted the partners to adopt specific balancing practices. These practices enabled a change process that was incremental and fragile in progression, yet resilient in its cumulative pattern. We develop a process model that explains the dynamics of collaborative change and shows how balancing change and stability enables partners to progressively broaden and occasionally transcend collective‐individual alignment as trust and mutual understanding deepen. This study advances collaboration and paradox theory by exposing balancing practices tailored to collaborative settings that enable adaptation in dynamic environments and by proposing a gradual approach to navigating knotted paradoxes.

title: Recomposing Management Education Under Climate Crisis: Towards a Composting Heuristic for Epistemic Change
authors: Ling Li; Kate Seymour; Rosalyn Marron; Helena Kettleborough; Catherine Brentnall; Olivia Tomlinson; Sarah Walker; Nor Yusup; John Lever
affiliations: Department of Strategy, Enterprise and Sustainability Manchester Metropolitan University All Saints, Oxford Road Manchester UK
abstract: Abstract Management learning and education (MLE) is increasingly critiqued for its reliance on anthropocentric and profit‐maximization paradigms, which fail to adequately address the escalating ecological and climate crises. In this article, we call for an epistemic shift in MLE by introducing the metaphor of composting as a lens for collective reflexive critique. We propose a composting heuristic inspired by the social practices of managing organic matter—landfill, industrial composting and community composting—to help MLE educators critically examine the epistemic foundations, limitations and possibilities that shape their teaching and learning practices. This metaphorical framework highlights an epistemic transition towards a multispecies and regenerative pedagogical paradigm, grounded in relational ontology, care and embodied practice. We argue that engaging with the metaphor of composting—and reflecting critically on one's positioning within the landfill‐industrial‐community composting heuristic—can catalyse a collective endeavour to drive epistemic change in MLE in response to the urgent demands of climate and ecological breakdown.

title:
Everything everywhere all‐at‐once?
                    <scp>AI</scp>
                    , expertise–output decoupling, and new entrepreneurial strategy trade‐offs in the age of abundance
authors: Jen Gennai; Riitta Katila; Minu Kumar; Ian Sinapuelas
affiliations: T3 Consultants New York New York USA; Microsoft Redmond Washington USA; Google Mountain View California USA; Stanford University Stanford California USA; San Francisco State University San Francisco California USA
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Generative AI democratizes entrepreneurship by lowering barriers to ideation, creating an environment of abundance. Yet while AI produces speed, scale, and local autonomy, these benefits may come at hidden costs to output quality. Using illustrative vignettes to ground and elaborate, we particularly identify explainability, traceability, and generalizability as costs of abundance. As AI separates observable output from the expertise traditionally required to produce it, the entrepreneur's attention to evaluation becomes the scarce resource. We identify three trade‐offs and their interdependencies for entrepreneurs: speed‐to‐understanding, scale‐to‐oversight, and local autonomy‐to‐system‐wide relevance. Implications for human accountability of AI systems and governance (organizational design) challenges for entrepreneurs are discussed. Managerial Summary AI allows entrepreneurial firms to produce ideas and other outputs faster and at greater scale than ever before. As AI separates output from the expertise traditionally gained while creating it, the scarce resource shifts from generation to evaluation. This creates new managerial tensions: speed versus understanding, scale versus oversight, and local autonomy versus system‐wide relevance. These tensions help explain concerns about AI “going rogue”: simply keeping a human in the loop is not enough if the human expertise no longer includes the ability to understand, trace, question, and override the system. Entrepreneurs are challenged to design organizations that preserve meaningful human expertise and accountability.

title: Parental Response to Fetal Shocks and Macroeconomic Volatility
authors: Rakesh Banerjee; Farhan Majid
affiliations: Department of Economics, University of Exeter r.banerjee@exeter.ac.uk; mfarhanmajid@gmail.com
abstract: Abstract We examine parental response to a fetal shock using data from 150 Demographic and Health Surveys in 50 developing countries. Focusing on the impact of Ramadan fasting, a common shock experienced by more than a billion Muslims worldwide, we find that children exposed to Ramadan fasting during pregnancy have lower rates of full vaccination for DPT and polio compared to their non-exposed siblings. Further, parents tend to compensate for the fetal shock during booms and reinforce during economic downturns. Our estimations suggest that this has resulted in approximately half a million excess infant deaths over the past three decades.

title: The Female Sensitivity Hypothesis: Evidence From Experimental Economics
authors: Felipe A. Araujo; Neeraja Gupta; Lise Vesterlund
affiliations: Lehigh University; University of Richmond; University of Pittsburgh and NBER
abstract: Abstract We assess the empirical evidence for the hypothesis that women more than men respond to changes in treatment. First, we examine whether the results of over two hundred experimental economics papers support the female sensitivity hypothesis. Second, using data from two studies (DellaVigna and Pope, 2022; Exley et al., 2025), we conduct over two hundred pairwise tests of the hypothesis. Both analyses show that gender is not predictive of responsiveness to treatment. We further examine how the hypothesis has been disseminated in the literature and find that it is referenced predominantly by papers that support it.

title: The Equilibrium Effect of Information in Consumer Credit Markets: Public Records and Credit Redistribution
authors: Scott L. Fulford; Éva Nagypál
affiliations: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau Scott.Fulford@cfpb.gov
abstract: Abstract Information is central to consumer credit, but little is known about its equilibrium effects. We study a 2017 natural experiment in which non-bankruptcy public records were purged from U.S. credit reports. The large information-removal differences across states allow us to identify equilibrium impacts. Available credit increased for consumers who lost negative information directly. Consistent with our model, available credit declined indirectly for consumers who did not lose the negative information because they could no longer distinguish themselves. The direct and indirect effects nearly canceled, so the net equilibrium effect after a year was nearly zero but with substantial redistribution.

title: Hostility, Population Sorting, and Backwardness: Quasi-Experimental Evidence from the Red Army after WWII
authors: Christian Ochsner
affiliations: CERGE—EI Prague, CESifo, SIAW at the University of St. Gallen, and University of Lucerne. CERGE-EI—A joint workplace of Charles University and the Economics Institute of the Czech Academy of Sciences, Politickych veznu 7, 111 21 Prague, Czech Republic, Phone: +420 224 005 173 christian.ochsner@cerge-ei.cz
abstract: Abstract How can short episodes of localized hostility shape regional economic trajectories that even amplify over time? I exploit economic differences across the idiosyncratic and short-lived line of contact between the Red Army and the Western Allies in South Austria at the end of WWII. The 74-day hostile presence of the Red Army shaped the age- and occupation-structure via refugee flows, causing amplifying demographic effects over time and backwardness in sector development and tax revenues. My findings also point to the isolated role of the Red Army’s hostile actions after WWII in understanding the European economic East-West divide.

title: Structuring Cash Transfers: Cash Flow Preferences, Seasonality, and Financial Decisions in Rural Kenya
authors: Carolina Kansikas; Anandi Mani; Paul Niehaus
affiliations: University of Cambridge; University of Oxford; UC San Diego
abstract: Abstract We examine the preferences of low-income households in Kenya over the structure of unconditional cash transfers. Most preferred lumpy transfers, and some preferred deferred receipt—in contrast to the typical structures of safety-net programs, but consistent with evidence on the financial challenges of poverty. Turning to consequences, receiving transfers later in the year raised income 1.5 years later—but willingness to defer receipt was sensitive to small changes in cash flow around the time of decision-making. Taken together, these results illustrate how adapting cash transfer design to the decision-making environment of those in poverty could improve financial choices and outcomes.

title: Blended Finance and Female Entrepreneurship
authors: Halil İbrahim Aydın; Çağatay Bircan; Ralph De Haas
affiliations: CBRT Halil.Aydin@tcmb.gov.tr; Amazon and UCL bircanca@amazon.co.uk; EBRD, KU Leuven, and CEPR dehaasr@ebrd.com
abstract: Abstract We study the real and allocative consequences of relaxing gender-specific credit constraints by analyzing a blended finance program designed to expand bank lending to female entrepreneurs in Turkey. Merging credit registry, tax, and matched employer-employee data, we find participating banks raised their credit share to women by over 18%, spanning repeat, poached, and first-time borrowers. Beneficiary firms invest more, grow employment, sales, and profits, diversify their networks, and exit less. Treated banks also expand lending to male entrepreneurs, though the increase is smaller and disproportionately directed toward higher-productivity firms, suggesting reallocation rather than crowding out. District-level effects are absent, reecting the program’s modest scale.

title: How Credible Are the Findings from Online Experiments?
authors: Abel Brodeur; Nikolai Cook; Anthony Heyes; Lamis Kattan
affiliations: University of Ottawa abrodeur@uottawa.ca; Wilfrid Laurier University ncook@wlu.ca; University of Birmingham a.g.heyes@bham.ac.uk; Georgetown University in Qatar lk811@georgetown.edu
abstract: Abstract Online experiments have surged in popularity, but how credible are their published results? We examine the universe of hypotheses tested on Amazon Mechanical Turk and reported in leading journals between 2010 and 2021. We find evidence of widespread p-hacking, publication bias, and under-powered studies. The extent of the problems varies substantially across fields, with marketing particularly badly afflicted and little evidence of distortion in economics. We explore correlates of increased credibility and compare the online results to laboratory results from the same outlets, finding similar distortions in both, with bunching just above the significance threshold more pronounced on MTurk.

title: Tax Incentives and Return Migration
authors: Jacopo Bassetto; Giuseppe Ippedico
affiliations: University of Milan, IAB, RF Berlin; University of Nottingham, CESifo, IZA, RF Berlin
abstract: Abstract We study how tax incentives affect the return migration of high-skilled expatriates to their home country, exploiting a generous income tax break for returnees in Italy. Using administrative data and a Triple-Difference design, we estimate a migration elasticity to the average net-of-tax rate just below one. Responses are sizable across the upper half of the earnings distribution, indicating that tax-induced migration is not limited to top earners. A cost-benefit analysis reveals that, while costly in the short term, the scheme pays for itself in present value if a sufficiently large fraction of returnees remains after the scheme elapses.

title: Contracting Structures in Public Procurement: Evidence from Donor-Funded Electrification in Kenya
authors: Catherine D. Wolfram; Edward Miguel; Eric Hsu; Susanna B. Berkouwer
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology and NBER; University of California, Berkeley and NBER; University of California, Berkeley; University of Pennsylvania and NBER
abstract: Abstract We study how contracting and monitoring structures in public procurement affect large-scale infrastructure construction. Starting in 2016, Kenya’s public electric utility ran competitive auctions and then awarded and administered dozens of procurement contracts to connect millions to electricity. The causal analyses leverage natural and experimental variation and granular, independentlycollected construction quality data. Kenya Power contracts funded by the World Bank featured unbundled contract components known as ‘design-bid-build’ and enhanced monitoring compared to African Development Bank-funded contracts. Unbundling contracts delayed construction progress but improved quality. Randomized inspections improved quality without large delays. Bundled contracting with additional independent monitoring could improve outcomes.

title: Is American Soft Power a Casualty of the Trade War? Evidence from U.S. Movie Viewership in China
authors: Haichao Fan; Yichuan Hu; Lixin Tang; Shang-Jin Wei
affiliations: School of Economics, Fudan University, Shanghai, China fan_haichao@fudan.edu.cn; School of Economics and Management, Tongji University, Shanghai, China huyichuan175@gmail.com; Institute for Economic and Social Research, Jinan University, Guangzhou, China lixintang@jnu.edu.cn; Columbia University, New York, New York, USA shangjin.wei@columbia.edu
abstract: Abstract The US trade war against China can either enhance or diminish American soft power in China, depending on whether Chinese citizens view it as legitimate. We study how US movie viewership, a measure of American soft power, responds to the trade war. We find a significantly greater reduction in US movie viewership in regions more exposed to the Trump tariffs, but no corresponding decline in non-US movies. The decline is stronger for action and drama movies, which tend to embody greater perceived “Americanness.” Survey data also show a sharper decline in trust in Americans in more tariff-exposed regions.

title: Semiparametric learning from open-set label shift data
authors: Siyan Liu; Yukun Liu; Qinglong Tian; Pengfei Li; Jing Qin
affiliations: East China Normal University KLATASDS-MOE, School of Statistics, , Shanghai ,; University of Waterloo Department of Statistics and Actuarial Science, , Waterloo, ON ,; National Institutes of Health National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, , Bethesda, MD ,
abstract: Abstract We study the open-set label shift problem, where the test data may include a novel class absent from the training data. This setting is challenging because both the class proportions and the distribution of the novel class are not identifiable without extra assumptions. Existing approaches often rely on restrictive separability conditions, prior knowledge, or computationally infeasible procedures, and some may lack theoretical guarantees. We propose a semiparametric density ratio model framework that ensures identifiability while allowing overlap between novel and known classes. Within this framework, we develop maximum empirical likelihood estimators and confidence intervals for class proportions, establish their asymptotic validity, and design a stable Expectation–Maximization algorithm for computation. We also develop a goodness-of-fit test for model assessment and an approximately optimal classifier with theoretical guarantees. Simulations and a real-data application confirm that our methods improve both estimation accuracy and classification performance compared with existing approaches.

title: Multi‐Agent Contracting With Network Externalities
authors: Yang Sun; Wei Zhao
affiliations: School of Economics Southwestern University of Finance and Economics Chengdu China; School of Economics and Management Tsinghua University Beijing China
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper analyzes how the structure of externalities‐encompassing both pure spillovers and interactive components‐reshapes the classic trade‐off between incentives and risk in multi‐agent contracts. The interplay of network effects and moral hazard generates congestion effects among agents with a common neighbor, which we decompose into a sum of weighted Katz‐Bonacich centralities. This tractable characterization enables clear comparative statics on the externality structure. We further apply the framework to examine how organization structures shape firm boundaries, and the design of Pigovian taxes to generate social security.

title: Cognitive ability, risk preferences and errors
authors: Michalis Drouvelis; Graeme Pearce
affiliations: University of Birmingham; CESifo, Munich; University of St Andrews
abstract: Abstract In this paper we examine the link between cognitive ability, risk preferences and the errors that people make. We build a unique dataset that contains almost 260,000 decisions made under risk in a variety of tasks by approximately 13,000 individuals, with each person having completed a test designed explicitly to measure their cognitive ability. Our analysis suggests that intelligence has (1) no impact on risk preferences and (2) a robust link to errors. Our results have implications for the development of theories that seek to explain the impact of cognitive ability on decision making.

title: Professional Networks and the Labour Market Assimilation of Immigrants
authors: Olof Åslund; Mattias Engdahl; Sébastien Willis
affiliations: Uppsala University; Institute for Evaluation of Labour Market and Education Policy (IFAU); Uppsala Center for Labor Studies; Centre for Research and Analysis of Migration (CReAM); Rockwool Foundation Berlin
abstract: Abstract We examine how professional networks shape immigrants’ job search and labour market assimilation. Analysing displaced workers in Sweden, we show that connections to firms through conationals are especially important for immigrants’ job finding. As networks expand to include more natives, the value of such connections rises towards that seen for displaced natives. Origin homophily also predicts whether a connection provides a referral—increasing earnings and lowering turnover—rather than vacancy information. Networks account for 20 per cent of the growth in immigrants’ re-employment over their first decade after arrival; immigrants’ networks are as productive as natives’ after fifteen years.

title: Excess Movement in Option‐Implied Beliefs
authors: NED AUGENBLICK; EBEN LAZARUS
abstract: ABSTRACT We derive bounds on the rational variation in option‐implied beliefs about market returns. While risk preferences distort option‐implied (or risk‐neutral ) beliefs away from subjective beliefs, one can nonetheless bound risk‐neutral belief movement under a general assumption on the stochastic discount factor. The resulting test requires no knowledge of the objective distribution and allows significantly more flexibility in discount rates than standard volatility tests. Implementing our test empirically using index options, we find that there is so much movement in risk‐neutral beliefs that the bounds are routinely violated. Our results imply significant excess index‐price volatility.

title: The Rise of Alternatives
authors: Juliane Begenau; Pauline Liang; Emil Siriwardane
affiliations: Stanford GSB, NBER, and CEPR ,; Georgia Tech ,; Harvard Business School and NBER ,
abstract: Abstract Since the 2000s, U.S. public pension funds have actively shifted their risky investments away from public equities and toward alternative assets like private equity and hedge funds—some much more than others. We explore a range of possible explanations for these trends and argue that beliefs about the risk-adjusted return of alternatives have played a central role. Pension beliefs are shaped by investment consultants, peers, and experience in the 1990s. Other demand-side channels related to risk-seeking motives, spending needs, and fund governance have weaker empirical support. We also consider supply-side factors and agency interpretations of the data. (JEL G11, G23, G41, H75)

title: The Economics of Data Unions: Optimal Data Sharing and Coordination
authors: Lin William Cong; Simon Mayer
affiliations: Nanyang Technological University, ABFER, and NBER; Carnegie Mellon University , Tepper School of Business
abstract: Abstract We develop a model of data-driven competition in which product quality depends on users’ data contributions and firms’ investments in data infrastructure. Users’ inability to internalize the value generated by their data, together with firms’ strategic investment incentives, can lead to data underinvestment—limiting quality—or overinvestment—concentrating market power. We introduce a data union that coordinates users’ contributions and can be implemented through a data trust or intermediary that aggregates user data. By shaping data compensation, the union enables users to capture and internalize more of their data’s value, enhancing user welfare, especially when combined with data sharing among firms. We apply these insights to financial data, digital payments, and Open Finance. Our analysis shows that data portability can strengthen competition but, without coordination, may leave data investment too low or excessive.

title: Corporate Tax Changes and Credit Costs
authors: Yota D. Deli; Manthos D. Delis; Iftekhar Hasan; Panagiotis N. Politsidis; Anthony Saunders
abstract: Abstract We examine changes in the state corporate tax rate across the U.S. and their implications on the pricing and quantity of loans. We find that the cost of credit decreases by approximately 10 basis points following a tax cut. When we account for the magnitude of tax changes, a one‐percentage‐point tax cut (hike) is associated with a 10.5 (9.2) basis‐point decrease (increase) in loan spreads. Our findings mainly originate from the demand side: large firms are able to mitigate the effects of tax increases, while less profitable firms experience larger reductions in borrowing costs following tax cuts. The effect on the equilibrium loan amount is statistically and economically insignificant, consistent with a weak supply effect and an inelastic loan supply curve.

title: Enabling Employee Adaptability to Change: The Joint Effect of Compensation Contract and Process Accountability
authors: Marte Abts; Martine Cools; Sabra Khajehnejad; Alexandra Van den Abbeele
affiliations: Erasmus University Rotterdam; KU Leuven
abstract: ABSTRACT Organizations increasingly operate in uncertain environments, requiring employees to revise task strategies to remain effective. We examine how pay for performance (PFP) influences adaptive performance following unanticipated change and argue that process accountability moderates this effect. Although PFP increases effort, it hinders adaptation by reinforcing persistence with an existing task strategy. Process accountability channels PFP-induced motivation into deeper strategic deliberation, enabling adaptation. We test our predictions in an experiment manipulating compensation (PFP versus flat wage) and process accountability (absent, reflection-only, and present), with participants in the reflection-only condition privately reflecting on their decision-making to isolate the social-evaluative component. Results show that PFP, relative to a flat wage, decreases adaptive performance when process accountability is absent, has no significant effect under reflection-only, and increases it when process accountability is present. Additional analyses suggest that strategic deliberation partially explains this effect. The findings underscore pairing PFP with process accountability to foster adaptation. title: Capital Market Pressure and Racial Inequality in Labor Violations
authors: Seth S. Carnahan; Sarah E. McVay; MaryJane R. Rabier
affiliations: Washington University in St. Louis; University of Washington
abstract: ABSTRACT Managers can boost reported earnings to meet capital market expectations by pursuing aggressive cost-minimization strategies that violate labor laws, such as pressuring frontline employees to forgo safety protocols or work off the clock. We investigate whether labor law violations, which benefit the firm at the expense of employees, fall disproportionately on nonwhite frontline employees. Across similar locations (e.g., stores or plants) within the same firm, we predict and find that locations with a higher share of nonwhite frontline employees are more likely to experience a labor law violation. This racial inequality in labor violations is especially pronounced in settings more prone to racial discrimination and during periods of acute capital market pressure to meet earnings benchmarks, providing insight into the mechanisms underlying the observed disparity. Our evidence suggests that capital market pressure is associated not only with labor violations but also with racial inequality in exposure to those violations. Auditors' Response to Clients' Cyber Breaches: A Human‐Capital Perspective
authors: Bing Li; Yifu Li; Jeffrey Pittman; Wenfeng Wang
affiliations: Department of Accountancy City University of Hong Kong Kowloon Hong Kong; Department of Accounting Renmin University of China Beijing China; Faculty of Business Administration, Memorial University St. John's Newfoundland and Labrador Canada; Department of Accounting and Information Systems Virginia Tech Blacksburg Virginia USA; Department of Accounting Southern University of Science and Technology Shenzhen China
abstract: ABSTRACT Using online job postings data, we explore whether auditors adjust their human capital in response to clients' cyber breach incidents. We find that audit offices increase their demand for cybersecurity specialists after their clients' cyber breaches, implying that cyber breaches change not only client risk but also their auditor's production function. Consistent with expectations, we document that this impact is larger when breaches involve their own clients (rather than those of peer offices within the same audit firm) and when breaches directly involve financial information. Our evidence holds for both cyber‐focused and non‐cyber‐focused offices, highlighting the broad impact of cybersecurity risks on audit practices. Additionally, we find that audit offices with relatively high investment in cybersecurity human capital are better able to preserve their market share among clients in high‐cyber‐risk industries after a client's cyber breach.

title: The Symbolic Politics of Housing
authors: DAVID E. BROOCKMAN; CHRISTOPHER S. ELMENDORF; JOSHUA L. KALLA
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley; University of California, Davis; Yale University
abstract: Voter opposition to development contributes to America’s housing shortage. Prevailing explanations emphasize NIMBYism (opposition to housing nearby) and homeowners’ self-interest. However, homeownership often fails to predict housing policy views, while NIMBYism offers little insight into support for policies that do not concern specific proposed housing projects—the focus of much recent policymaking. Drawing on symbolic politics theory, we argue that voters’ affect toward groups that housing policies make salient powerfully shapes their judgments about housing policies. We present evidence supporting this theory. Experiments show that affect toward developers and investors who build housing, government actors who approve it, and residents who move into it explain anti-development preferences when policies make these groups salient. Providing further causal evidence, short-form videos that manipulate affect toward developers have meaningful downstream effects on support for new development and permitting reforms. Ironically, voter dislike of the very actors who could ameliorate the housing shortage further exacerbates it.

title: Structure and agency in emancipatory reform: A blueprint from a Black union
authors: Benjamin T. Lynerd
affiliations: Department of Political Science Christopher Newport University 1 Avenue of the Arts Newport News Virginia USA
abstract: Abstract The National Labor Convention of 1869, the first of its kind for African American workers, yielded a grand strategy for achieving full emancipation, in which those long subjected to domination might attain durable independence. Drawing upon decades of Black republican thought, this agenda combined macro‐level reforms targeting agrarian and industrial monopolies with micro‐level interventions into the habits of the working class. While the project fell short, its multivalent approach nevertheless offers republican theorists today a framework for better understanding the structural dynamics of domination and how to overcome them.

title: Learning traps
authors: Hassan Sayed
affiliations: Market Shaping Accelerator Center for Global Development, Washington DC USA
abstract: Abstract When constituents are uncertain about whether leaders' policy preferences align with their interests, policy choices generate a trade‐off between payoffs and information. Leaders can experiment with their preferred policy, but if the outcome is bad, constituents learn this and threaten office removal. I use a repeated model of political agency to analyze how this trade‐off shapes long‐lived, term‐unlimited leaders' policy choices. When there is uncertainty about the optimal policy for constituents, leaders implement “learning traps”: spatially intermediate policies that halt learning about what the best policy is. They experiment only when their preferences are very likely to be aligned with constituents, a contrast to the “gambling for resurrection” logic ubiquitous in the literature. I provide a case study that examines how the 1861 reforms ending Serfdom in Imperial Russia represented the logic of a “learning trap” and illustrate additional applications of the model to political contagion and economic policymaking.

title: War and Welfare in Colonial Algeria – ERRATUM
authors: Gabriel Koehler-Derrick; Melissa M. Lee
